A dark page that keeps growing

  1. Dark paper. Turn the gradient on. It must switch to the Night palette by itself. If the text goes dark on this dark background, the automatic switch is broken — and that is not a subtle failure, it is an unreadable page.
  2. Deliberate choice wins. Pick Mono in the popup. It must stay on Mono, mixed from this page's own light ink towards its dark paper. The switch is only allowed to override a palette meant for light paper.
  3. New content. Press Append three paragraphs. They should colour by themselves within about half a second, without touching anything that was already painted.
  4. Replaced content. Press Replace the article. Everything old goes and everything new should get coloured, which is the case a single-page app hits on every navigation.
  5. Re-render in place. Press Re-render paragraph 1 in place. Its colour vanishes for a moment and must come back within about half a second. If it stays plain, the extension has lost that paragraph for good — which is what happened before this check existed.
  6. Partial re-render. Press Insert a word into paragraph 2. A new sentence appears at the end and the whole paragraph must be recoloured, the new sentence included. Nothing was removed here, so this only works if the extension notices the text got longer.
  7. Narrow the window. Drag it thinner. Lines break in new places and the colour must follow, by re-measuring rather than re-wrapping.
  8. Turn it off. Everything, appended paragraphs included, must go back to plain.

Sites with their own dark mode are the case where painting blindly does the most damage. Every palette meant for white paper is built out of colours dark enough to read against white, which is to say colours that vanish against this. Getting it wrong here does not produce a slightly worse effect; it produces a paragraph the reader cannot see at all.

So the paper gets measured rather than assumed. The extension walks up from the article container until it finds a background that is actually painted — backgrounds are usually transparent all the way to the body — works out its luminance, and switches palettes if it is dark. The ink is read the same way, because the strength slider mixes towards the page's own text colour and a page like this one has light ink.

The same measurement feeds the contrast floor. Every colour stop is pulled back towards the ink until it clears four and a half to one against whatever paper was found, so a palette cannot quietly hand somebody grey text on a grey background, and the palest stop of the lightness-only palette adapts instead of being wrong on half the web.
